subject: biology
title: Biology MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock A (8 tasks, 72 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1 | A 6]]
A student studies a leaf under a microscope.
Diagram not to scale. [Description: a printed micrograph of one palisade mesophyll cell from a leaf. The cell is a tall rectangle containing a thin cell wall, a large central vacuole, many green chloroplasts around the edge of the cytoplasm, and a nucleus. The student measured the length of the cell on the printed micrograph as 48 mm. The magnification of the micrograph is x600.]
(a) Identify the structure that controls the activities of the cell. (1 mark)
(b) Explain why palisade cells contain many chloroplasts. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the actual length of the cell. Give your answer in micrometres (1 mm = 1000 micrometres). (2 marks)
(d) State the level of organisation of a whole leaf. (1 mark)

Total for Question 1: 6 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Nucleus [1]. (b) Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy [1]; more chloroplasts means more photosynthesis, so more glucose is made (accept: more light is absorbed) [1]. (c) Actual length = image length / magnification = 48 / 600 [1] = 0.08 mm = 80 micrometres [1] (award both marks for 80 with no working; 0.08 mm without conversion gets 1). (d) Organ [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 2 | A 7]]
A grassland ecosystem contains the following feeding relationships. Grasshoppers and rabbits eat grass. Frogs eat grasshoppers. Snakes eat frogs. Hawks eat snakes and rabbits. Foxes eat rabbits.
(a) State the producer in this ecosystem. (1 mark)
(b) Write down the longest food chain in this ecosystem. (1 mark)
(c) State the trophic level of the frog. (1 mark)
(d) A disease kills most of the rabbits. Predict and explain the effect on the number of snakes in the short term. (2 marks)
(e) The grass in one area stores 50 000 kJ of energy each year. Assuming that 10% of the energy is transferred at each step, calculate the energy available to the frogs. (2 marks)

Total for Question 2: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Grass [1]. (b) Grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk (arrows pointing in the direction of energy flow; accept a correct chain written with arrows) [1]. (c) Secondary consumer (accept third trophic level) [1]. (d) Snake numbers decrease [1] because hawks, which now have fewer rabbits to eat, eat more snakes [1]. (e) Grass to grasshopper = 5 000 kJ [1]; grasshopper to frog = 500 kJ [1] (award both marks for 500 kJ with no working).

questions.content:
[[Q 3 | A 7]]
Amylase is an enzyme in saliva that breaks down starch. A student mixes amylase with starch solution at six temperatures and records the time taken for all the starch to disappear (tested with iodine solution).
Temperature in degrees Celsius: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
Time for starch to disappear in seconds: 240, 120, 60, 30, 90, no change after 600
(a) Identify the temperature, from those tested, at which amylase works fastest. (1 mark)
(b) The rate of reaction = 1 divided by the time taken. Calculate the rate at 20 degrees Celsius, in units of per second. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why there was no change at 60 degrees Celsius. (2 marks)
(d) State the name of one product of the digestion of starch by amylase. (1 mark)
(e) Explain why the time taken falls between 10 and 40 degrees Celsius. (1 mark)

Total for Question 3: 7 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) 40 degrees Celsius [1]. (b) Rate = 1 / 120 [1] = 0.0083 per second (accept 8.3 x 10 to the power minus 3) [1]. (c) The high temperature breaks the bonds that hold the enzyme in shape, so the active site changes shape (the enzyme is denatured) [1]; the starch no longer fits the active site so the reaction cannot happen [1]. (d) Maltose (accept sugar or glucose) [1]. (e) Enzyme and substrate particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so there are more frequent collisions with enough energy to react [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 4 | A 8]]
A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before feeling pain.
(a) Put the following parts of the reflex arc in the order in which an impulse passes through them: effector, relay neurone, receptor, motor neurone, sensory neurone. (2 marks)
(b) State one reason why reflex actions are important. (1 mark)
(c) Compare nervous and hormonal communication by stating two differences. (2 marks)
(d) Before a race, a cyclist's heart rate increases because a hormone is released. Name the gland that releases this hormone. (1 mark)
(e) Explain how this hormone helps the cyclist to perform well. (2 marks)

Total for Question 4: 8 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) Receptor first and effector last [1]; sensory neurone, then relay neurone, then motor neurone in the middle in that order [1]. (b) They are fast and automatic, so they protect the body from harm (accept: no time needed for decisions) [1]. (c) Any two differences from: nerves use electrical impulses, hormones are chemicals carried in the blood; nervous responses are fast, hormonal responses are slower; nervous effects are short-lived, hormonal effects last longer; nervous effects are local, hormones can affect many target organs [1][1]. (d) Adrenal gland (accept adrenal glands) [1]. (e) Adrenaline increases the heart rate so more blood is pumped per minute [1]; more oxygen and glucose reach the muscles for aerobic respiration, releasing more energy for movement [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 5 | B 10]]
A class wants to investigate how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in the water plant Elodea. A student places a piece of Elodea in a beaker of water, with a lamp at a measured distance from the beaker. The student counts the bubbles of gas released from the cut end of the stem in one minute.
(a) State a research question that this investigation could answer. (2 marks)
(b) Formulate a testable hypothesis, using scientific reasoning. (2 marks)
(c) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(d) Describe how the student can change the light intensity and obtain reliable values for the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(e) Outline one variable that must be controlled, and how this can be done. (1 mark)
(f) Outline one safety precaution for this investigation. (1 mark)

Total for Question 5: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A question linking both variables, for example: How does the distance of the lamp from the Elodea (light intensity) affect the number of bubbles released per minute? [2] (1 mark if both variables are named but not linked). (b) A prediction that links the variables, for example: as the lamp is moved closer, more bubbles will be released [1]; with reasoning, for example: more light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll, so photosynthesis is faster and more oxygen is produced [1]. (c) Independent: distance of lamp from the plant (light intensity) [1]; dependent: number of bubbles per minute (rate of oxygen release) [1]. (d) Use a metre rule to place the lamp at several set distances, for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm [1]; at each distance count the bubbles for the same period, repeat at least three times and calculate a mean (accept: allow the plant to adjust for a few minutes before counting) [1]. (e) Any one from: temperature, using a water bath or a heat shield (heat-absorbing water tank) between lamp and beaker; carbon dioxide concentration, by adding the same amount of sodium hydrogencarbonate; same piece of Elodea or same length of stem; room darkened so other light does not interfere [1]. (f) Any one from: do not touch the hot lamp; keep electrical equipment away from water; wipe up spills; wash hands after handling pond plants [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 6 | C 10]]
The class results are shown. Three trials were done at each distance.
Distance of lamp in cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Bubbles per minute, trial 1: 48, 25, 16, 9, 6
Bubbles per minute, trial 2: 50, 27, 15, 8, 6
Bubbles per minute, trial 3: 46, 26, 29, 10, 6
(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one possible cause. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute at 30 cm, leaving out the anomalous result. (2 marks)
(c) The means for the other distances are 48, 26, 9 and 6. State which variable should be plotted on the horizontal axis of a graph of the means. (1 mark)
(d) Describe the trend shown by the means. (1 mark)
(e) Explain the trend using your knowledge of photosynthesis. (2 marks)
(f) Evaluate one limitation of counting bubbles to measure the rate of photosynthesis, and suggest an improvement. (2 marks)

Total for Question 6: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) 29 bubbles at 30 cm in trial 3 [1]; a possible cause, for example miscounting, the lamp being moved closer, or the water warming up [1]. (b) (16 + 15) / 2 [1] = 15.5 bubbles per minute [1]. (c) Distance of the lamp (independent variable) [1]. (d) As the distance increases, the mean number of bubbles per minute decreases (the decrease is steep at first and then levels off) [1]. (e) Further from the lamp there is less light energy for the chlorophyll to absorb [1], so photosynthesis is slower and less oxygen gas is released as bubbles [1]. (f) A limitation, for example bubbles vary in size so counting does not measure the volume of gas accurately, or some oxygen dissolves or is used in respiration [1]; an improvement, for example collect the gas in a capillary tube or gas syringe and measure its volume [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 7 | D 10]]
Read the passage.
A farming cooperative in East Africa is deciding whether to grow insect-resistant maize. Scientists have inserted a gene from a soil bacterium into the maize so that the plant makes a protein that is harmful to stem-borer caterpillars. In field trials the yield increased by 20% and the farmers sprayed insecticide twice a season instead of six times. The seed is patented, so farmers must buy new seed each year at three times the price of ordinary seed. Some consumers worry about long-term health effects. Some ecologists worry that pollen could carry the new gene to wild relatives of maize.
(a) Outline what is meant by genetic modification. (2 marks)
(b) Describe two benefits of growing the insect-resistant maize. (2 marks)
(c) Explain one possible environmental risk of growing the insect-resistant maize. (2 marks)
(d) Discuss one economic or social factor that the cooperative should consider. (2 marks)
(e) Justify whether the cooperative should grow the maize, using evidence from the passage. (2 marks)

Total for Question 7: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A gene from one organism is transferred into the genome (DNA) of another organism [1]; so that the receiving organism has a new characteristic (makes a new protein) [1]. (b) Any two from: higher yield, so more food or income [1]; less insecticide used, which saves money and reduces pollution and harm to other insects and farm workers [1]. (c) Pollen carries the gene to wild relatives [1], which may change wild populations or let weeds gain resistance to pests, reducing biodiversity (accept: the toxin may harm non-target insects such as butterflies, or caterpillars may evolve resistance) [1]. (d) Economic: seed costs three times as much and must be bought every year, which may put the cooperative in debt or make farmers depend on one company [1], balanced against the extra income from the 20% higher yield (accept a social factor such as consumer acceptance or access to seed for poor farmers, with a development) [1]. (e) A clear decision [1] supported by evidence from the passage, for example yield rises by 20% and spraying falls from six to two times, which may outweigh the seed cost if prices are high enough (accept a reasoned decision against, citing the cost or ecological worry) [1].

questions.content:
[[Q 8 | A 6 | C 4 | D 4]]
Read the passage and study the data.
Measles is caused by a virus that spreads in droplets from coughs and sneezes. In a population with no immunity, one infected person passes the virus on to about 15 others (R0 = 15). The two-dose measles vaccine is about 97% effective. Town Y recorded its vaccination coverage and the number of measles cases each year.
Year: 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022
Children fully vaccinated (%): 98, 97, 90, 82
Measles cases in the town: 3, 6, 95, 240
(a) Explain how a vaccine gives a person immunity to a disease. (3 marks)
(b) The percentage of a population that must be immune to stop an outbreak spreading is given by 100 x (1 - 1/R0). Show that this is about 93% for measles. (2 marks)
(c) Describe the changes in vaccination coverage and in the number of cases in Town Y between 2016 and 2022. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why the number of cases rose in Town Y even though most children were still vaccinated. (3 marks)
(e) Some parents refuse to vaccinate their children. Discuss the ethical and social factors involved in making vaccination compulsory. (4 marks)

Total for Question 8: 14 marks
questions.mark_scheme: (a) A vaccine contains weakened or dead pathogens, or their antigens [1]; white blood cells (lymphocytes) recognise the antigens and make specific antibodies [1]; memory cells remain, so if the real pathogen enters later, antibodies are made much faster and in larger amounts [1]. (b) 100 x (1 - 1/15) [1] = 100 x 0.933 = 93.3%, so about 93% [1]. (c) Coverage fell from 98% to 82% [1]; cases rose from 3 to 240 (accept: cases rose steadily each time coverage fell) [1]. (d) By 2020 coverage (90%) had fallen below the 93% needed for herd immunity [1], so there were enough unvaccinated people for the virus to keep passing from person to person [1]; the vaccine is also not 100% effective, so some vaccinated children were still susceptible, and as more people became infected the virus spread faster [1]. (e) Ethical: compulsory vaccination limits personal and parental choice (autonomy) [1], but protects babies and people with weak immune systems who cannot be vaccinated and rely on herd immunity [1]. Social: reduces illness and healthcare costs for the whole community, but may reduce trust in health authorities or punish families unfairly, whereas education about vaccine safety may persuade more people [1]. A balanced judgement or conclusion supported by reasoning [1].
